q: Which equation shows the basic accounting equation?
r: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity
Everything a business owns is funded by debt or by the owner.
w: That formula is closer to net income than to the balance sheet.
This reverses the relationship between the elements.
This mixes balance sheet and income items.

q: What is an asset?
r: A resource a business owns that has value
Cash, inventory and equipment are examples.
w: An amount a business owes to others
A cost a business pays to operate
Money the owner takes out for personal use

q: What is a liability?
r: A debt or obligation owed to an outside party
Accounts payable and loans payable are examples.
w: Something of value that the business owns
The owner's claim on business resources

q: Which account is an example of an asset?
r: Equipment
Equipment is owned by the business and has value.
w: This is a liability owed to suppliers.
This is an expense on the income statement.
This is revenue earned from customers.

q: Which account is an example of a liability?
r: Notes Payable
A note payable is money the business must repay.
w: This is an expense, not a debt.

q: In double-entry accounting, every transaction affects at least how many accounts?
r: Two
Each transaction has a debit side and a credit side.
w: A single account cannot keep the equation balanced.
Some entries do, but at least two is the rule.
This is not required for every transaction.

q: On which side of a T-account is a debit recorded?
r: The left side
Debits go left and credits go right.
w: Credits are recorded on the right.
T-accounts are split left and right.
Each entry is on one side only.

q: What is the normal balance of an asset account?
r: Debit
Assets increase with debits.
w: Credit is the normal balance of liabilities.
Asset accounts usually carry a balance.
Either side, depending on the month
Normal balances do not change from month to month.

q: What is the normal balance of a revenue account?
r: Credit
Revenue increases with credits.
w: Revenue builds up during the period.
Normal balance is fixed by account type.

q: What is the normal balance of an expense account?
r: Debit
Expenses increase with debits.
w: Credit balances are normal for revenue.

q: Marcus starts Marcus Mowing by depositing $5,000 of his own money into a business bank account. How is the transaction recorded?
r: Debit Cash, credit Marcus, Capital
Cash increases and the owner's equity increases.
w: This would show the owner withdrawing money.
The deposit is not income from customers.
No customer owes the business money here.

q: Birch Bakery buys $400 of flour on account. Which accounts are affected?
r: Supplies increases and Accounts Payable increases
The business gains supplies and owes the supplier.
w: No cash was paid yet because it was bought on account.
Buying supplies does not create revenue.
Accounts Payable decreases and Cash decreases
This would show paying a debt.

q: A business pays $300 cash for a bill it received last month for office supplies. What is the effect?
r: Assets and liabilities both decrease by $300
Cash goes down and accounts payable goes down.
w: Cash is paid out, so assets do not increase.
The expense was already recorded when the supplies were bought.
Paying a liability does not change equity.

q: A customer pays $250 for a repair completed today. Which entry is correct?
r: Debit Cash, credit Service Revenue
The business receives cash and earns revenue.
w: The customer paid right away, so nothing is owed.
The business does not owe anything here.

q: Which statement about the accounting equation is true after every transaction?
r: The equation stays in balance
Both sides change by the same total amount.
w: Assets always exceed liabilities plus equity
The two sides must stay equal.
Many transactions do not affect liabilities.
Many transactions only move amounts between assets.

q: A business has assets of $60,000 and liabilities of $22,000. What is owner's equity?
r: Equity equals assets minus liabilities.
w: This adds liabilities instead of subtracting them.

q: The owner withdraws $800 from the business for personal use. What happens?
r: Cash decreases and owner's equity decreases
A withdrawal reduces both the asset and the owner's claim.
w: Owner withdrawals are not business expenses.
This describes an investment by the owner.
The business does not borrow when the owner withdraws money.

q: Which principle says a business should record revenue when it is earned, not necessarily when cash is received?
r: Revenue recognition
Revenue is recorded in the period in which it is earned.
w: This assumes the business will continue operating.
This values assets at their original purchase cost.
This concerns how large an item must be to matter.

q: What does the matching principle require?
r: Expenses are recorded in the same period as the revenue they helped earn
This shows an accurate picture of profit for the period.
w: All revenue is recorded when cash arrives
The matching principle concerns revenue and expenses.
Each debit matches a credit in a different period
Entries balance in the same period.

q: Under the cost principle, how is land bought for $90,000 that is now worth $130,000 recorded?
r: At $90,000, the original purchase price
Assets are recorded at cost, not at current market value.
w: Market value increases are not recorded under the cost principle.
At $110,000, the average of the two
Averages are not used for recording assets.
Only the original cost is recorded.

q: Why must a business keep personal and business finances separate?
r: The business entity concept treats the business as its own unit
Records then show only what the business itself did.
w: The law forbids owners from using any bank
No law forbids owners from banking.
Personal expenses are always tax deductible
Banks charge less for separate accounts

q: Which concept assumes a business will keep operating into the foreseeable future?
r: Going concern
Assets are recorded as if the business will keep using them.
w: This concerns using the same methods over time.
This concerns reporting all relevant information.

q: A bookkeeper uses straight-line depreciation in year one and a different method in year two for the same asset. Which concept is violated?
r: Consistency
Methods should stay the same so results can be compared.
w: This concerns separating owners from the business.
This concerns dividing activity into periods.
This concerns recording assets at cost.

q: What is the purpose of a chart of accounts?
r: To list all the accounts a business uses, with account numbers
It gives bookkeepers a consistent filing system.
w: To show the business's profit for the year
To record each customer's payment history
That is a customer subsidiary record.
To list the owner's personal investments
The chart covers business accounts only.

q: Account numbers beginning with 1 in a typical chart of accounts usually represent which type?
r: Assets
The common numbering order is assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, expenses.
w: These usually start with 5 or higher.

q: What does a trial balance prove?
r: Total debits equal total credits
It checks the arithmetic of the ledger.
w: Profit is measured on the income statement.
A trial balance can still balance with missing entries.
All entries were posted to the right accounts
Posting to wrong accounts can still balance.

q: A trial balance shows debits of $18,400 and credits of $17,900. Which error would most likely explain the difference?
r: A $500 debit was posted but its matching credit was not
The missing credit leaves debits higher by $500.
w: A $500 debit was posted to the wrong debit account
That would make credits higher, not lower.
Both sides were recorded using the wrong date

q: A $450 debit was posted as $540 to one account and the credit was correct. What is the difference in the trial balance?
r: Debits exceed credits by $90
The debit side was overstated by $90.
w: The debit, not the credit, is too large.
The error is only the difference between 540 and 450.
The totals are no longer equal.

q: A transposition error occurs when two digits are swapped. Which sign suggests this error?
r: The difference is evenly divisible by 9
Swapped digits always produce a difference that divides by 9.
w: The difference is an odd number
Odd differences can have many causes.
The difference equals one of the account balances

q: Which transaction increases both assets and owner's equity?
r: The owner invests additional cash in the business
Cash goes up and the owner's claim goes up.
w: The business buys supplies for cash
The business borrows money from a bank
Assets and liabilities increase, not equity.
The business pays a utility bill
Assets decrease when this bill is paid.

q: Which transaction does NOT change total assets?
r: Buying a computer for cash
One asset increases while another decreases by the same amount.
w: Cash increases and so do total assets.

q: What does the term 'revenue' mean?
r: Income earned from selling goods or services
It is the money flowing in from business activity.
w: Costs paid to run the business

q: What does the term 'expense' mean?
r: A cost incurred to earn revenue
Rent, wages and utilities are common expenses.
w: An amount owed to a supplier

q: What is net income?
r: Revenue minus expenses
It is the profit left after all costs are covered.

q: If expenses are greater than revenue for a period, the business has a:
r: Net loss
Costs exceeded income.
w: Profit requires revenue to exceed expenses.
Equity is a balance sheet measure.

q: What is the accounting cycle's first step?
r: Analyze transactions from source documents
Every entry starts with evidence of a transaction.
w: Statements come near the end of the cycle.
Closing happens at the end of the cycle.

q: Which is a source document?
r: A sales receipt
It provides evidence that a transaction happened.
w: This is a summary used to check totals.
This is a list of account names.

q: Where are transactions first recorded in chronological order?
r: The journal
The journal is the book of original entry.
w: This is a report, not a record of entry.
This is a report of results.

q: What is posting?
r: Transferring journal entries to ledger accounts
Posting updates the balance of each account.
w: Writing the first entry from a receipt

q: Which is the correct order of the first three steps of the accounting cycle?
r: Analyze, journalize, post
Evidence leads to journal entries, which are posted to the ledger.
w: Posting uses the journal, so it cannot come first.

q: What is the difference between cash-basis and accrual-basis accounting?
r: Accrual records revenue and expenses when earned or incurred; cash records them when money moves
Accrual gives a better picture of performance.
w: Both methods record all account types.
Accrual specifically records unpaid bills as liabilities.
Neither basis is defined by double entry.

q: A salon provides a service on March 28 and is paid on April 5. Under accrual accounting, when is the revenue recorded?
r: March 28
Revenue is recorded when it is earned.
w: That is when cash is received, as under the cash basis.
Whichever month is cheaper to report
Timing is set by the principle, not by choice.

q: An electric bill arrives on December 28 but is not paid until January 10. Under accrual accounting, the expense belongs to:
r: December
The expense was incurred when the electricity was used.
w: That is when it is paid, as under cash accounting.
Expenses must be recorded in some period.
An expense is recorded only once.

q: What is a compound journal entry?
r: An entry with more than two accounts
Some transactions need several debits or credits.
w: An entry that is repeated each month
An entry that corrects a mistake

q: What is the purpose of a general ledger?
r: To hold all accounts and their balances in one place
It is the main record from which statements are prepared.
w: Sales are only part of the ledger.
To record the original source of each transaction
That is the role of the journal.
That belongs in a customer database.

q: What is a contra account?
r: An account with a balance opposite to its related account
Accumulated Depreciation offsets an asset.
w: An account used only by auditors
Contra accounts are part of ordinary records.
An account that is always zero
It carries a balance that offsets another account.

q: Which accounts are called temporary accounts?
r: Revenue, expense and drawing accounts
They are closed at the end of each period.
w: Any account with a small balance
Balance size does not decide the type.

q: Why are temporary accounts closed at period end?
r: So each new period starts at zero
Revenue and expenses are measured period by period.
w: So that they cannot be audited
Closed accounts remain available to auditors.
To remove assets from the ledger

q: A business has revenue of $52,000 and expenses of $41,500. After closing, what increases by the net income?
r: Owner's capital
Net income is transferred to owner's equity.
w: Closing entries do not change cash.
Expense accounts are reduced to zero.
